_comment: The contract between the Java engine and the report's client-side evaluator.
Phase 2 lets a tester tune a threshold in the browser and watch the verdict recompute, then
save the file so the next run gates on it. That only means anything if the two evaluators
agree — and two independently written implementations drift between the runs that test them.
So neither owns the definition: this file does. AssertionParityTest runs it in Java and a
Playwright spec runs it in the browser, and both must produce the statuses below.
Add a case here whenever either side gains behaviour. A case that only one side can pass is
the bug this file exists to catch.
A case's `expect.attainment` (AF5b) is how much of the fail band the rule used, as
Attainment.of and the page's Budget column (attainmentFor) compute it: the worst match's actual,
the fail threshold, the fraction consumed and whether the fail band fired - or null where the
question does not apply (no fail band, a rule that decided nothing, a divisor of zero). Java
had AttainmentTest and the page nothing but one fixture's bar colour; AssertionParityTest,
asserts-parity.test.js and asserts-parity.spec.ts now hold both to these.
_errorSummariesComment: What ErrorSummary aggregates, in the shape the payload ships. errorClass is computed once
in Java by ErrorClass.of() and carried as a field, so the browser reads it rather than
re-deriving — there is one classifier, not two that can drift.
checkout has 45 errors: 20 protocol (503), 15 non-protocol (a 200 JMeter still failed),
10 transport. They sum to the errorCount the sampler reports, which is what makes
class= a partition rather than a second opinion.

_comment: A child sampler's errors, which whole-run scope must not count. The code was the
literal string CHILD-ONLY, chosen as a label rather than as data — and it derives to
transport, while this row states protocol. Java derives; the browser reads the stated
token from the payload. So the two evaluators were being handed different data by the
file that exists to stop exactly that, and no assertion compared them until the
harness started cross-checking these two fields.
It is 500 now: a real code that derives to the class it declares, and the same code as
its parent, which is what a transaction child would actually carry.

_extraPercentilesComment: Quantiles off the standard p50/p75/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 grid, as the retained digest would
answer them. Java reads them through a PercentileSource; the browser reads them from the
p85 is here because the two sides used to key this map differently and only a fractional
percentile ever proved it: Java wrote String.valueOf(85.0) — '85.0' — and the browser asked
for String(85), which is '85'. The lookup missed, a miss is NaN, and a rule the engine
passed rendered INVALID in the report. p97.5 spelled identically on both sides, so the
vectors that existed could not see it. A whole number is the case that matters.
The keys in E notation are RB8's: GatePayloadBuilder.percentileKey files a quantile below
0.001 under Double.toString's spelling, 1.0E-4, where String(1e-4) is '0.0001', and the
subnormal 4.9E-324 under Java's two digits, where String() writes '5e-324'. The page looked
both up by String() and missed, so a rule the run judged read NO_VALUE on the page.
99.99999999999999 is the last double below 100, which a hex spelling rounds to.

_why: RB8 (a): how a percentile is SPELLED. MetricRef.parse trims the name (String.trim: every char
up to U+0020 and nothing else), lower-cases it, and reads what follows the p through
Double.parseDouble, which trims again and takes Java's whole floating-point grammar: a sign,
digits with a point anywhere, an exponent, an f/F/d/D suffix, a hex float. The page's
parseMetric read /^p(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)$/ and called every other spelling INVALID_RULE, so a rule
the run judged read INVALID on the page after any edit. Java owns the run, so the page now
reads the percentile through WIR.javaText.parseDouble, Java's grammar, and names it as
canonicalPercentileName does. `expect.metric` is the canonical name every runner checks: the
one GatePayloadBuilder ships, and the one ruleFromJson must arrive at from the file's spelling.

server assert's requiresLoad/divideBy finds its rule by that name. AssertionRuleMapper.readTarget
is the definition: a blank or empty value is not a form, more than one form is INVALID (picking
one would judge something nobody asked for), and scope is compared case-insensitively. An

derived one. ruleFromJson read {samplers: []} as 'group-...', {scope, sampler} as the scope,

(sampler, samplers, match, overall, invalid), `expect.id` the id the rule is judged under,
`expect.problem` an INVALID target's whole sentence. MapperParityTest runs these through the
mapper, asserts-parity.test.js and asserts-parity.spec.ts through ruleFromJson.

_bandTextCasesComment: L2 / CN25: a band written as TEXT, read as AssertionRuleMapper reads it - through
ServerMetricsMapper.asNumber, which trims with String.trim, parses with Double.parseDouble and
refuses NaN and the infinities. The page's bandNumber read the text with trim() and Number(), so
"0x10" was 16, "0o17" was 15 and a no-break space was trimmed, where Java refuses all three,
and "1d" and "0x1p3" were refused where Java reads 1 and 8. Since K a band Java refuses is
carried and written back, so the editor read "0x10" as a band, offered no refusal, and an
unedited Save turned the row from INVALID into a page verdict (CN25).
Each `text` is the value of `fail: {gt: ...}` on a mean rule. `expect.value` is the band Java
reads, compared exactly; `expect.refused` means Java refuses it as the text it is, in
Usability.unreadableBand's whole sentence. MapperParityTest runs these through the mapper,

_migrationCasesComment: M5 exploratory F1: the legacy loadValidity block, migrated into assertions[] as the run
migrates it (ReportAnnotations.migrateLegacyBlocks -> LoadValidityMigration). The page used to
read a file's assertions[] and nothing else, so Open file... on E25's own annotations file showed
one rule fewer than the report - and a Download then dropped the load check altogether, because
the page never writes loadValidity back. Each case is a whole document; `expect.assertions` is
the list Java ends with, compared by value (a null field and an absent one alike, as Jackson
binds them). MapperParityTest runs these through AnnotationLoader's mapper and the migration;
asserts-parity.test.js and asserts-parity.spec.ts through the page's migrateLoadValidity.

_why: L3 / CN26: a target or a tolerance that is not a finite number. Jackson binds a Double from a
number or from text - trimmed, "NaN", "Infinity", "-Infinity" and its own "INF" and "-INF"
included, and the rest through Double.parseDouble - and a bare 1e400 is Infinity by the time
it is bound. The run migrated such a block into a rule whose band no measurement can be
compared with, refused in the mapper's words for a band (`fail lt must be a number, not the
number NaN`) that name nothing the file wrote; an infinite target wrote (long) Infinity into
the description; a -Infinity target read as a target at or below zero and declared nothing;
and a -Infinity tolerance was clamped to 0, a band of the target itself that the run judged.
The page's jacksonDouble read text only by /digits/, so a "NaN" target migrated nothing and a
Download dropped the load check, and a "NaN" tolerance migrated to a judged `lt target`.
Now the migration builds the rule, never clamps a non-finite tolerance, and refuses each band
it could not build with a sentence naming the field; `expect.detail` is the migrated rule's
INVALID_RULE detail, and a non-finite band is written as Jackson writes it, as text. The
runners read the migrated rule through the production parser on both sides: the mapper and
Usability.refusal in MapperParityTest (which also wants a finding naming the field),
ruleFromJson and whyUnusable in asserts-parity.test.js and asserts-parity.spec.ts.
